chapter: Becoming a musician: ukulele, clarinet and the Boozaire Kings
title: Boyhood jobs: shoe shines, papers, pounding red brick
summary: Danny describes the hustles of a Black boy: shining shoes, selling papers, working with peddlers and pounding red brick for sidewalk decoration.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Everybody was so nice to the musicians. You're something special. You see that. So what the hell you gonna do? Now, you're a youngster, a Black youngster in New Orleans, and you figure, well, what'cha gonna do? From a kid you start shining shoes. You never even think of stealin' or takin' nothin' from nobody. You're not (?). You get a shoe-shining box, you can sell papers...
Go to work, yeah. Work.
Yeah. You can work piling brick. You can work for the grocery store...
What do you mean piling brick?

You get red bricks, and you pile it, because people use it to clean their sidewalk. And you'd take this brick and pound it, then you'd pound it, and then sprinkle this brick, and when you'd walk, it... It would smash(?) and give a coloring to the front of your house.
To the front of your house.
Yeah.
Barker - I-52
And kids would pound it up into powder at the time.
Yeah, powder it.
Get with the (?).

Yeah. You'd powder it... You'd say you were going to pound some bricks. So you'd wait until you see... If a kid in my neighborhood... If you saw a pretty red brick with a soft brick, an old ancient brick, you know, or even the plaster part of it. But you could tell, because the brick is almost pinkish, it's so pure, made out of this red sand. But it's red brick. And not a fire brick; a fire brick is hard. But this brick is...
Porous.

Yeah, it's porous. And you'd bring that brick home, because later, on Saturday, you'd see some bricks in the street. Or if they were building and they were knocking down the pillars, and then you go in the foundation you'd take two or three of them bricks. Because you could always sell a bucket of bricks to somebody in your family. See, you got six or seven ...(?)...
You'd get you a big old stone or something, and just pound it up til...
Then you'd get a hammer and you'd get a stone, and you'd take the brick and you'd wet it, and you'd
Barker - I-53

put it in the bucket wet. Then when you hit it, it cracks quick. And then you just pound the brick. You don't pound it into a powder. You pound it into a small grain by a little digging(?) in the rice and the pea and the bean.
Oh, I see. And then they spread it all on the sidewalk in front of the house.

And then throw it around after they've washed the steps, and then they use the yellow ochre. I don't know what the hell that was, but you could buy that yellow ochre at the grocery store. So when they washed the steps, they'd throw this yellow ochre in the bucket. And when they scrubbed them steps with the lye or whatever it was, high-powered soap or cleanser... It was a yellow octagon(?) soap. And the yellow ochre and that would make the steps be steps...as the pure wood, but it would have a yellow tinge. It's a decorating thing. And then they... All around the South, the bricks are even and everything, because people keep their bricks in front. You'd sprinkle that brick around there, and it makes a nice picture.
Oh yeah. Like little stones around there.

Yeah. But you see, when you step on them, it makes a powder and it's spread. So when you've done that, you sold papers. And you went and you worked with a peddler on Saturdays -- Fridays and Saturdays you worked with a
Barker - I-54

peddler, and he might give you fifty cents. You had your little spending change. And it wasn't so easy to spend your money like kids today. I see kids with two or three dollars, and they throw it in the pinball machine. There's no way in the world you could have got me, hard as I had to hustle for that money, to go playin' no pinball machine. I'd wait until the ice cream comes, get my ice cream, then when the doughnut man comes, get me a doughnut...
Yeah.
And I wanted to go to the show.
Yeah!
